ap_calculus_ab-m01.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the graph of $f(x)=3 e^{\cos(2x)}$ at the point where $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$?

options.why: By the chain rule $f'(x)=3\cdot e^{\cos(2x)}\cdot(-2\sin(2x))$; at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$ we have $\cos(2x)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\sin(2x)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $f'=- 3 \sqrt{3} e^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
Omits the inner derivative: it differentiates $\cos(2x)$ as $-\sin(2x)$ and leaves out the factor $2$.
Treats the derivative of $e^{u}$ as just $u'$ and drops the factor $e^{\cos(2x)}$.
Uses $\sin(2x)$ instead of $-\sin(2x)$ as the derivative of $\cos(2x)$, so the sign is wrong.

blueprint.subject: ap_calculus_ab
blueprint.concept: Differentiate an exponential of a trigonometric function with the chain rule and evaluate at an exact point
student_thinking: Identify the outer function $e^{u}$ and the inner function $u=\cos(kx)$
Multiply the outer derivative $e^{u}$ by the inner derivative $-k\sin(kx)$
Evaluate at the given angle using exact trigonometric values

misconceptions.description: forgets the factor k from the inner derivative
drops the minus sign of the cosine derivative

verification.independent_path: central difference (step 1e-6) of the lambdified function at the numeric point (independent of the symbolic chain rule)

ap_calculus_ab-m02.stem: Let $f(x)=x^{5}+x$, which is one-to-one, and let $g$ be the inverse function of $f$. What is the value of $g'(2)$?

options.why: Evaluates the derivative at the wrong place: $\frac{1}{f'(2)}$ instead of $\frac{1}{f'(1)}$.
Divides by $[f'(1)]^{2}$ instead of by $f'(1)$, giving $\frac{1}{[f'(1)]^{2}}$.
Takes $f'(1)$ and forgets to use its reciprocal.

blueprint.concept: Find the derivative of an inverse function at a point when the function is given by a formula

misconceptions.description: squares the derivative in the denominator

verification.independent_path: root-finding for $f(z)=b\pm h$ and a central difference of the numerical inverse (independent of the formula $1/f'$)

ap_calculus_ab-m03.stem: Let $f(x)=\ln\left(\cos{\left(x \right)} + 4\right)$. Which of the following is $f'(x)$?

options.why: Multiplies $u'$ by $u$ instead of dividing by $u$.
With $u=\cos{\left(x \right)} + 4$ and $u'=- \sin{\left(x \right)}$, the chain rule gives $f'(x)=\frac{u'}{u}$.
Differentiates $\ln u$ as $\frac{1}{u}$ and forgets to multiply by $u'$.
Reverses the sign of the inner derivative $u'$.
